instructions:
Read the paper below and produce a structured summary.

It matched these tracked topics; `relevance` must contain one entry per slug, stating what this paper changes for that topic:
- overthinking: Overthinking — When and why large reasoning models think more than a problem needs (or less than it needs) — the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff of reasoning length, test-time compute scaling, and methods to make a model stop, or keep going, at the right point.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what

payload.title: Strategic Scaling of Test-Time Compute: A Bandit Learning Approach

contributions: Formulates test-time compute allocation across queries as a bandit learning problem
Adaptive algorithm that estimates query difficulty online and allocates more compute to harder queries while preserving accuracy on easier ones
Identifies solvable-but-hard instances to avoid wasting compute on effectively unsolvable queries
Theoretical guarantees of improved efficiency over uniform compute allocation
result.method: Casts the problem of distributing a test-time compute budget across a stream of queries as a bandit learning problem. The algorithm adaptively estimates each query's difficulty as it goes and allocates more compute (more reasoning/sampling effort) to harder queries and less to easier ones, while also trying to detect instances that are difficult but effectively unsolvable so compute is not wasted on them.
methods: bandit learning algorithm for compute allocation
result.one_liner: Formulates test-time compute allocation across queries as a bandit learning problem so that harder queries get more compute and easier ones get less.
result.problem: Allocating test-time compute uniformly across all queries is wasteful: easy queries receive more compute than they need and very hard (possibly unsolvable) queries can consume large amounts of compute without a proportional accuracy gain.

relevance.overthinking: Directly targets the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff at the center of the topic by adaptively deciding, per query, how much test-time compute to spend based on estimated difficulty, rather than a fixed budget applied to every query regardless of need.

result.results: Roughly 11 percentage points (about 15% relative) improvement on MATH-500, about 10.8 points (14.4% relative) on AIME25, and about 11.2 points (15.3% relative) on LiveCodeBench, compared to uniform compute allocation.
